summary: Letting a node choose a forwarding path other than the shortest one benefits many network functions, yet earlier source-based routing mechanisms saw little adoption. This informational RFC gives the SPRING problem statement and requirements, where source means where the explicit route is imposed.

eli5.summary: Writing down the route a package should take instead of letting each post office decide. This explains why and what is needed.

questions: what is source packet routing in networking
how does spring solve traffic engineering
can spring work with non-spring routers
subtitle: Enabling networks to specify explicit packet routes instead of shortest paths

tldr.problem: Network operators need to direct traffic along specific paths for traffic engineering, fast recovery, and network programmability, but existing source-routing methods have seen limited adoption.
tldr.mechanism: SPRING (Source Packet Routing in Networking) proposes an architecture where the source node (ingress point, not necessarily the packet originator) encodes the forwarding path directly in the packet header, avoiding the need for per-hop signaling.
tldr.outcome: This enables operators to implement traffic engineering, fast reroute, network virtualization, and SDN control with minimal network state, supporting both MPLS and IPv6 data planes.

facts.label: Key architectural principle
facts.value: Policy in packet header, not network state

today: RFC 7855 remains the authoritative problem statement and requirements document for the SPRING architecture. Subsequent RFCs (such as RFC 8402 on Segment Routing Architecture) have implemented SPRING concepts, making this RFC a foundational reference for understanding source packet routing on modern networks.

sections.title: Why Networks Need Source Routing
sections.content:
Normally, each router forwards a packet along the shortest path to the destination, computed using routing protocols like OSPF. However, network operators need more control for several reasons: network virtualization, link protection, traffic engineering, and network programmability.

Previous source-routing mechanisms (where a source specifies the path) have existed but saw little adoption. SPRING is designed to address this gap. The term "source" here means the point where an explicit route is imposed—typically the network ingress point, not necessarily the original packet sender. SPRING aims to support these use cases without requiring massive network upgrades or a "flag day" where everything changes at once.
sections.eli5: Routers usually pick the fastest route automatically. But sometimes network operators want to pick a specific route for safety or to balance load. SPRING lets them write that route in the packet.

sections.title: Key Use Cases for SPRING
sections.content:
The RFC describes four main problem areas. IGP-based MPLS tunneling allows virtual private networks (VPNs) to tunnel traffic from one edge router to another without signaling protocols in the core. Fast Reroute (FRR) precomputes backup paths to quickly bypass failed links or nodes. Traffic Engineering lets operators steer specific flows along particular paths based on bandwidth, topology, or other constraints. Interoperability requires SPRING nodes to coexist with non-SPRING nodes, enabling gradual deployment.

Traffic engineering use cases are especially detailed: dual-plane networks need to route traffic within a single plane for disjoint paths; egress peering traffic engineering controls which upstream providers are used; load balancing across non-parallel links lets operators distribute traffic unevenly with weighted multi-path forwarding.
sections.eli5: Network operators want to: protect important traffic, fix broken links fast, balance load across the network, and handle virtual private networks. Each of these benefits from being able to choose the route.

sections.title: How SPRING Works
sections.content:
SPRING encodes the explicit forwarding path in the packet header itself, so intermediate routers do not need to store state about the path. This is a key advantage: the network does not need to maintain per-flow, per-service, or per-policy state on midpoint routers. The policy lives only at the ingress node that imposes it.

SPRING is designed to work with existing data planes: MPLS (using the label stack) and IPv6 (using a new IPv6 routing header). MPLS data plane uses the label stack to encode the path, while the IPv6 data plane uses a Segment Routing Header (SRH) to carry path segments. Both must support interoperability with non-SPRING-capable nodes. The approach avoids additional signaling protocols; the network uses only existing IGP and BGP control planes.
sections.eli5: Route instructions are packed into packets like directions on an envelope. Routers read the instructions and forward accordingly. SPRING works with both MPLS and IPv6 networks.

sections.title: Architectural Requirements
sections.content:
The SPRING architecture must meet several key requirements. It MUST allow incremental deployment without synchronizing all nodes. It MUST put policy state in the packet header, not on intermediate nodes, so midpoints and tail-end routers need no special configuration for each flow. It SHOULD be general enough to work with multiple data planes.

For traffic engineering, SPRING must support both loose routing (where only key hops are specified) and strict routing (where every hop is explicit). It must work with centralized controllers (SDN) and distributed path computation. It must support bandwidth admission control, ECMP awareness, and disjoint paths in dual-plane networks. Fast reroute must work on any topology without additional signaling.
sections.eli5: SPRING must be safe to add to existing networks gradually, keep route instructions in packets rather than routers, and support many different ways operators want to manage traffic.

sections.title: Security and Trust Boundaries
sections.content:
Since SPRING encodes the path in the packet, an attacker could potentially manipulate the traffic path by modifying the packet header or injecting false routing instructions. The RFC requires clear trust domain boundaries: source-routing information must be usable only within the trusted domain and never exposed outside.

An assumed trust model holds that any node imposing an explicit route is allowed to do so. This is stricter than plain IP but consistent with existing traffic-engineering techniques. At domain boundaries, routers must filter SPRING routing information to prevent leaks. For IPv6, the RFC proposes using cryptographic signatures to authenticate paths. Control-plane security is also critical: an attacker controlling the SDN controller could manipulate traffic paths.
sections.eli5: Because SPRING lets someone choose the route, the network must trust the source of those instructions. If an attacker changes the instructions, they could hijack traffic.
